newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Italy renounces production, export of landmines.
newsitem.headline: Italy renounces production, export of landmines.

text.p: Italy, a key producer of mines, said on Thursday it would would end "once and for all" the production and export of anti-personnel landmines.
In his speech to the General Assembly, Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said the Italian government "pledges to renounce once and for all the production and export of anti-personnel landmines."
He said Rome would also begin destroying existing devices "in the hope that such measures will contribute to reaching a solid international understanding and a definitive ban."
"We hope this will contribute to a broader understanding and lead to an international ban on production of landmines," he told a news conference later.
Italy has been singled out by the United Nations as a key producer of the 110 million landmines planted worldwide, along with China, Bulgaria and other nations.

A U.N.-sponsored conference in Geneva agreed to limit the use of some landmines in May, but stopped short of a ban because some countries argued they should remain a legitimate form of military defence.
Following the 55-nation Geneva conference, the United States said in May it would seek a global ban on landmines by the year 2001. Almost 40 other nations support a total ban.
The Geneva conference agreed to outlaw undetectable anti-personnel mines and is due to reconvene in the year 2001 to consider progress and possible further moves.
But critics say the agreement encourages the use of more advanced mines which will still be permitted in the meantime.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, in his Tuesday speech to the General Assembly renewed his appeal "for the swift negotiation of a worldwide ban on the use, stockpiling, production and transfer of anti-personnel mines. Our children deserve to walk this earth in safety."

And Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, whose country holds the European Union presidency and speaks for the bloc, said that 110 million landmines had been sown worldwide, disabling a quarter of a million people.
Germany banned export of mines in 1994 and France said last year it would stop production of all anti-personnel mines and start destroying its stocks.

Angolan Foreign Minister Venancio de Moura told the U.N. General Assembly on Monday that there were over 10 million mines in his country alone and that more than 10,000 people had been mutilated by them.
